**Authors:** Matthew Truwit and Matthew Ronfeldt  
**Venue:** Educational Evaluation and Policy Analysis, 2026, DOI: [10.3102/01623737261453349](https://doi.org/10.3102/01623737261453349)  
**Review Date:** 2026-09-25  
**Model:** GPT-6 via Codex  
**Review Mode:** Retrospective (Reader's Guide)

### Overall Assessment: Useful With Caveats

This paper supplies useful evidence about conversion to self-described teacher residencies among existing, predominantly undergraduate Tennessee preparation programs. Its within-program design improves on simple comparisons between residency and traditional graduates, and its treatment checks document changes in preparation. The published estimates do not demonstrate average improvements in graduate racial diversity, Tennessee public-school employment, or workforce retention (p. 12, Table 3); they do not establish that meaningful benefits are absent. Positive mobility and instructional-effectiveness findings are suggestive, with outcome-specific pre-trend concerns, imprecision, and selective observation limiting causal confidence. My assessment is that the study deserves selective citation as evidence about incremental program conversion, rather than a verdict on comprehensive residencies or particular program components. The literature positioning and reporting need qualification, and weak reproducibility limits independent verification without itself demonstrating that the estimates are wrong. Readers should retain the useful local evidence while avoiding the stronger claims about proven teaching-quality gains, effects fading with experience, or lower bounds on comprehensive implementation.

#### Key Strengths

- A policy-relevant within-program comparison: the imputation difference-in-differences estimator accommodates staggered adoption and heterogeneous effects, using untreated observations to construct counterfactuals and clustering inference by program (pp. 7–8). This is a meaningful design improvement over cross-program comparisons, conditional on its identifying assumptions.
- Treatment validation goes beyond the residency label: adoption is associated with 95.90 additional supervised clinical hours (SE 35.67) in separately collected annual Title II reports (p. 10, Table 2, Panel B). This corroborates a change in preparation, although neither a full residency package nor a mechanism is identified.
- Linked administrative outcomes distinguish employment, workforce departure, school and district mobility, and instructional performance. The preferred post-completion observation window improves cohort comparability, and the bound appendix supplies composition and estimator checks (pp. 4–5; p. 12, Table 3; pp. 19–20, Tables A2–A3).
- The results and limitations sections disclose treatment uncertainty, incomplete implementation, restricted generalizability, and weaknesses in the positive findings (pp. 9–14, 17–18). These disclosures support a more careful reader interpretation than the concluding policy language alone.

#### Key Concerns

- Causal confidence differs by outcome: Table 3 reports pre-trend-test p-values of .022 for diversity, .010 for school mobility, and .079 for ELA value-added (p. 12). These are diagnostics of comparison trends, not treatment-effect p-values. My judgment is that the diversity and school-mobility interpretations are especially vulnerable, with ELA also warranting caution; estimator robustness cannot repair a deficient counterfactual.
- Treatment is retrospective, partial or full self-identification rather than a standardized intervention. Only 15 programs supply observed transitions, while always-residency programs do not identify adoption effects (p. 6, Table 1; p. 22, Figure A1; pp. 8–9). Limited variation, uncertain timing, and changing comparison-program practices constrain precision and generalization; attenuation and lower-bound interpretations are not established.
- Outcome populations and meanings are narrower than several substantive claims: graduate composition does not isolate recruitment; observed departures concern Tennessee public schools; mobility conditions on continued employment; effectiveness requires available evaluations or tested-subject assignments (pp. 4–5). Selection within these groups remains possible. Comparing observation windows does not isolate a common cohort’s career trajectory (p. 12, Table 3).
- The literature discussion overstates the distinctiveness of the design and compresses retention evidence. A relevant Louisiana adoption study already used implementation timing and program and completion-year controls, but is absent from the references (pp. 24–26; [Goldhaber, Xu, and Mihaly (2022), Box 2, pp. 5–6](https://ies.ed.gov/sites/default/files/migrated/rel/regions/southwest/pdf/REL_2023147.pdf)). The literature review’s concern about the Wan retention citation is also supported by the cited report; differing outcomes and follow-up periods make broad claims of contradicting prior research unreliable.
- The supplied article describes the design but provides no replication code, software environment, or actionable access route to the linked survey and administrative inputs. Reporting inconsistencies further impede reuse: p. 14 gives “up through 2015–2016, N = 9” and “in 2016–2017 or after, N = 6,” whereas Table A4 says “Earlier adopters are those (N = 6)” and “later adopters are those (N = 9)” (p. 21). Figure A1 supports the table’s counts (p. 22), but cannot establish the grouping used in estimation. These are verification limits, not proof that the aggregate estimates are incorrect; unavailable unbound supplements cannot be presumed to resolve them.

#### What to Rely On

- As a description of the published estimates, the study finds no clear average employment or workforce-retention improvement after the observed conversions: first-post-completion-year coefficients are 0.011 (SE 0.022) for employment and 0.005 (SE 0.009) for departure (p. 12, Table 3, Panels B–C). Cite this as an absence of demonstrated gains in Tennessee public schools, not an equivalence result.
- The diversity specification does not detect an improvement in graduating-cohort racial composition: its coefficient is −0.013 (SE 0.010; p. 12, Table 3, Panel A). This accurately describes the estimate, but the adverse pre-trend diagnostic prevents a confident conclusion that adoption cannot improve diversity.
- Reported conversion corresponds to some changes in preparation, including increased clinical hours (p. 10, Table 2). It is therefore informative about incremental adoption among existing providers, while the study’s own validation shows why residency labels should not be treated as uniform program packages.
- The paper offers a useful application of a staggered-adoption design to teacher preparation, with visible diagnostic and sensitivity evidence (pp. 7–8; p. 12, Table 3; p. 20, Table A3). Its contribution is additional evidence in this setting, not an established claim to being the first within-program adoption study.

#### What to Treat Cautiously

- Claims that adoption improves teaching quality: first-year ELA value-added is 0.031 student-level SD (SE 0.018), while observation ratings and math value-added are 0.032 (SE 0.033) and 0.034 (SE 0.024), respectively (p. 12, Table 3, Panel D; units in p. 13, Figure 2). The preferred evidence is imprecise, ELA has a pre-trend concern, and outcome coverage is selective; these are suggestive findings.
- Claims that adoption causes greater mobility: school and district mobility coefficients are 0.026 (SE 0.011) and 0.012 (SE 0.008), respectively, equivalent to 2.6 and 1.2 percentage points (p. 12, Table 3, Panel C). School mobility has a rejected pre-trend test, district mobility is only marginally significant, and both concern retained teachers rather than all completers.
- Claims that comparison teachers catch up or that the estimates bound comprehensive residency benefits: Table 3 contrasts “First year only” with “All available years” (p. 12), not matched experience trajectories. The lower-bound argument on pp. 11 and 18 requires assumptions about implementation and measurement error that the study does not establish; individual components are not separately identified.
- Adoption-cohort differences, special-education and partner-district follow-ups, and claims of addressing staffing shortages: the subgroup documentation conflicts, and several exploratory analyses lack full corresponding exhibits (pp. 12, 14–17; p. 21, Table A4). Certification does not itself show a vacancy was filled, and national career retention or cost-effectiveness is not measured.
- Compressed summaries of earlier evidence: the paper includes Wan et al. under “after 3 or more years” (p. 3), but the cited study examines retention into the second year and reports no statistically significant group differences within certification-status strata ([Wan et al. (2021), pp. 12–13, Figure 5 and accompanying text](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED612482.pdf)). Read the studies directly before citing a general residency-retention advantage or claiming this paper overturns it.

#### Verification notes

- CONFIRMED — Methods/contribution reviews: the clinical-hours estimate is 95.90 (SE 35.67), and the principal employment, departure, diversity, mobility, and effectiveness entries used above match the paper (p. 10, Table 2; p. 12, Table 3).
- CONFIRMED — Methods review: the diversity, school-mobility, and ELA diagnostic p-values are .022, .010, and .079; Table 3 explicitly identifies these as pre-trend tests (p. 12), distinct from treatment-effect significance.
- CORRECTED — The reviews leave adoption-group counts unresolved; counting transition rows in Figure A1 yields six earlier and nine later adopters (p. 22), supporting Table A4’s “Earlier adopters are those (N = 6)” / “later adopters are those (N = 9)” (p. 21), over p. 14’s “up through 2015–2016, N = 9” / “in 2016–2017 or after, N = 6”; the implemented estimation grouping remains unverified.
- CONFIRMED — Writing review: the captions say “Y-axis is in percentage points” and “Y-axis is measured in percentage points,” but binary panels show decimal ticks such as “.05” (pp. 11 and 13, Figures 1–2); by conversion, .05 is five percentage points.
- CONFIRMED — Writing/reproducibility reviews: the outcome definition says “across all 23 rubric items” (p. 5), while the discussion says “about half a point on 1 of 15 indicators” (p. 15; associated estimate in p. 12, Table 3, Panel D); the paper provides no reconciliation, so this guide does not reuse that illustration.
- CONFIRMED — Literature review: the omitted Louisiana report uses adoption timing with program and completion-year controls; this qualifies the contribution review’s novelty framing without negating the Tennessee application ([Goldhaber, Xu, and Mihaly (2022), Box 2, pp. 5–6](https://ies.ed.gov/sites/default/files/migrated/rel/regions/southwest/pdf/REL_2023147.pdf); omission checked against pp. 24–26 of the article).
- CONFIRMED — Literature review: the paper’s “after 3 or more years” characterization (p. 3) does not describe Wan’s retention horizon; the certification-stratum qualification is present in the source ([Wan et al. (2021), pp. 12–13, Figure 5 and accompanying text](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED612482.pdf)).
- COULD NOT CHECK — Reproducibility review: the underlying estimates, exploratory specifications, and code cannot be independently reproduced from the supplied materials; I confirmed the absence of an actionable replication/access statement in the article, but did not infer that no materials exist elsewhere. Online supplements and unbound appendices were unavailable.

### Methods Review
**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The paper uses a well-motivated staggered-adoption difference-in-differences design, credible administrative outcomes, and useful treatment-validation and estimator checks to study transitions by existing Tennessee teacher preparation programs. The evidence supports a cautious conclusion that these observed transitions did not deliver clearly demonstrated average improvements in employment or retention, but causal claims about diversity, mobility, and instructional effectiveness face outcome-specific pre-trend problems, selective outcome observation, and uncertain treatment timing. The design does not establish effects of comprehensive residency implementation, formal lower bounds on those effects, or a causal trajectory of benefits fading with teaching experience.

**Strengths:**

- The imputation estimator fits the staggered-adoption setting: program and graduating-year effects are estimated using untreated observations, avoiding reliance on already-treated programs as untreated comparisons and allowing heterogeneous treatment effects (pp. 7–8). This is a substantive improvement over cross-sectional comparisons between residency and traditional graduates.
- Statewide completer, personnel, and evaluation records provide complementary measures of graduate composition, employment, mobility, and performance. Focusing the preferred specification on the year immediately following completion substantially improves comparability of follow-up across graduating cohorts (pp. 4–5; p. 12, Table 3).
- The treatment indicator receives meaningful, though incomplete, corroboration: the estimated increase in supervised clinical experience is 95.90 hours, with SE 35.67, in separately collected annual Title II reports (p. 10, Table 2, Panel B). The authors also examine changes in reported model features rather than simply assuming that a residency label denotes a uniform intervention.
- Inference is clustered at the program level, matching the treatment-assignment unit, and the paper reports event studies and cluster-robust joint pre-trend tests rather than only aggregate coefficients (pp. 8, 12–13, Table 3 and Figure 2). The notes explain that pre-treatment and post-treatment coefficients use different reference constructions, an important interpretive distinction (p. 24, note 9).
- The bound appendix includes survey-response comparisons, cohort-composition checks, alternative estimators, and adoption-cohort estimates (pp. 19–21, Tables A1–A4). The authors explicitly acknowledge imperfect self-reported treatment, limited identifying variation, and the exclusion of always-residency programs from treatment-effect identification (pp. 9, 17–18).

**Weaknesses:**

- Parallel untreated outcome trends remain an assumption about the post-adoption counterfactual; passing a pre-period test cannot establish it. More consequentially, the joint pre-trend tests reject for candidate diversity (p = .022) and school mobility (p = .010), and raise concerns for ELA value-added (p = .079; p. 12, Table 3). These are directly relevant to the paper’s negative diversity interpretation and positive mobility and effectiveness interpretations. Other simultaneous program changes, local labor-market shocks, and changing graduate composition are not removed merely by program and year fixed effects.
- Treatment combines partial and full self-identification and retrospectively recalled adoption dates (pp. 4, 9; p. 23, note 2). Feature changes can precede the label, and traditional programs can adopt similar features (pp. 9–11, Figure 1; p. 16). My assessment is that this identifies a heterogeneous incremental transition relative to evolving alternatives, not a common residency package. Timing error and implementation differences need not bias every outcome toward zero, so the lower-bound interpretation on pp. 11 and 18 is not established.
- The justification that the imputation approach is robust to anticipation is too strong (p. 8; p. 24, notes 9–10). Using the whole pre-period can reduce dependence on an unusual final baseline year, but if substantive treatment effects begin before the recorded date, affected observations still enter the untreated fit. The displayed feature anticipation therefore leaves uncertainty about the appropriate onset of treatment; changing estimator alone does not resolve it.
- Workforce outcomes condition on employment, mobility additionally conditions on remaining employed, and effectiveness depends on having an evaluation or teaching a tested subject (pp. 4–5). Adoption could change who enters these observed subsets or their teaching assignments even without a statistically detectable change in overall employment. Consequently, performance and mobility differences cannot automatically be interpreted as effects for a fixed population of graduates. Composition checks on all completers do not settle selection within the employed, retained, or evaluated samples.
- Only 15 programs contribute observed transitions (p. 6, Table 1; p. 22, Figure A1). Program clustering is appropriate, but the effective treatment information remains limited, especially for adoption-cohort splits. No small-treated-sample inference check, program influence analysis, or multiplicity adjustment is reported. Marginal findings and isolated significant subgroup or event-time estimates therefore deserve less weight than the large individual-level sample sizes might suggest.
- The outcomes answer narrower questions than some substantive labels imply: graduate composition does not separately identify recruitment, enrollment, and completion processes; absence from Tennessee public schools does not establish departure from teaching nationally; and partner districts identified at the survey date are applied retrospectively (pp. 4–5; p. 23, note 4). These limitations particularly affect claims about recruitment mechanisms, professional retention, and historical partner-district placement.
- Pooling all available workforce years changes exposure lengths, experience composition, observation weights, and the set of employed teachers. Comparing that specification with first-post-completion-year estimates does not isolate within-teacher convergence over careers (p. 12, Table 3; p. 23, note 7). Similarly, Figure 2 combines changing sets of programs at different event times, as acknowledged on p. 11; its dynamics cannot by themselves establish maturation of the same programs.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Use the paper primarily as evidence about incremental changes at existing, predominantly undergraduate Tennessee programs that reported becoming residencies. Do not extrapolate its null or positive estimates directly to new, comprehensively implemented residencies, graduate pathways, or the always-residency programs excluded from identification (pp. 6–9, Table 1; p. 22, Figure A1).
- Read employment and retention results as an absence of clear average improvements under this design, rather than proof of no policy-relevant benefit. Keep the Tennessee public-school scope explicit and distinguish retention in the state workforce from staying in the same school or district (pp. 4–5; p. 12, Table 3).
- Treat the diversity conclusion and school-mobility increase as especially sensitive to the counterfactual trend assumption. Regard instructional-effectiveness gains as suggestive: their precision, ELA pre-trend concern, selective measurement, and variation across estimators preclude a firm conclusion that adoption improves teaching quality (pp. 12–14, Table 3 and Figure 2; p. 20, Table A3).
- Do not interpret larger first-post-completion-year coefficients as demonstrated fading effects with experience, or read the event-study curves as a fixed cohort’s improvement path. Those interpretations require comparable cohorts, exposure windows, and outcome-observation rules beyond the pooled contrasts supplied here (p. 12, Table 3; p. 13, Figure 2).
- Before building on adoption-cohort heterogeneity or exploratory partner-district and endorsement findings, verify subgroup definitions and the underlying specifications. The bound appendix documents the principal analyses, but the covariate-adjusted checks are described as unreported and several exploratory findings lack corresponding full exhibits; unavailable online materials cannot fill those evidentiary gaps (pp. 12, 14–17; p. 21, Table A4).

**Detailed Commentary:**

Assessment basis: I read the full article, including its bound appendix, notes, and references, and visually checked the principal outcome table, treatment-validation table, event-study figures, adoption-cohort table, and treatment-timing diagram. Reported estimates and reporting discrepancies below are verifiable from those materials; judgments about identification, selection, and interpretation are methodological assessments, not verified reanalyses. No underlying data or code were available for this review, and online supplements or appendices not bound into the PDF were not available.

The central estimand is an average effect for graduates of programs observed transitioning from their prior preparation practices to self-described residency practices. It is not the effect of each residency component, nor an estimate for the average institution independently of graduate counts: note 9 describes equivalence to program-by-year aggregation weighted by nonmissing graduate outcomes (p. 24). The Title II corroboration strengthens the interpretation that something substantive changed, but it does not identify clinical experience as the mechanism. Shared policy changes and the spread of residency features among comparison programs also make this a relative policy contrast. Observable cohort stability in Table A2 (p. 19) is reassuring without excluding unmeasured compositional change or changes in who completes the program.

For the principal null findings, the first-post-completion-year employment coefficient is 0.011 (SE 0.022), and the departure coefficient is 0.005 (SE 0.009; p. 12, Table 3, column 1). My rough normal-approximation intervals calculated from these rounded entries are approximately −3.2 to +5.4 percentage points for employment and −1.3 to +2.3 percentage points for departure. These are illustrative rather than exact cluster-adjusted intervals, but they demonstrate why a nonsignificant estimate is not an equivalence finding. The diversity estimate is −0.013 (SE 0.010), accompanied by the rejected pre-trend test already noted (p. 12, Table 3); the document establishes no detected diversity improvement in this specification, not a secure causal demonstration that transitions cannot improve diversity.

The positive findings have distinct vulnerabilities. School mobility increases by 0.026 (SE 0.011) in the preferred specification, but its own pre-period diagnostic challenges identification. ELA value-added increases by 0.031 student-level standard deviations (SE 0.018), while the observation-rating and math estimates are 0.032 (SE 0.033) and 0.034 (SE 0.024), respectively (p. 12, Table 3, column 1). Those latter estimates are imprecise, and the ELA result combines marginal statistical evidence with questionable pre-trends. Table A3 shows directional agreement across estimators, but not uniformly stable magnitudes: the alternative heterogeneity-robust math estimate is 0.096 (SE 0.033), compared with the preferred 0.034 (SE 0.024; p. 20, Table A3). My judgment is that this is useful sensitivity evidence, not a resolution of common identifying assumptions or proof of homogeneous effects. Evaluation missingness, testing disruptions, and assignment-dependent value-added coverage further narrow whose effectiveness is measured (p. 5; p. 23, notes 5–6).

There is a verified reporting discrepancy relevant to subgroup interpretation. In introducing Table A4, p. 14 describes earlier adopters as “up through 2015–2016, N = 9” and later adopters as “in 2016–2017 or after, N = 6.” The table note instead states “Earlier adopters are those (N = 6)” and “later adopters are those (N = 9)” (p. 21, Table A4). The text and table thus reverse the subgroup counts. This does not by itself invalidate the aggregate estimates, but the allocation should not be assumed resolved when using the heterogeneity results.

Overall, adequate is warranted because the study makes a meaningful design improvement, uses an estimator suited to staggered adoption, reports important diagnostics, and acknowledges substantial limitations. Its strongest contribution is a qualified challenge to assuming that favorable outcomes in exemplary residencies will follow from the transitions studied here. Claims that the residency model itself causes greater mobility or effectiveness, that effects necessarily attenuate with experience, or that estimates formally bound the benefits of full implementation carry substantially less evidentiary weight.

### Literature Review
**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The paper offers a useful, generally balanced account of residency research, especially variation across programs and the distinction between recruitment and preparation. However, it omits a close methodological predecessor and compresses some cited findings in ways that overstate both the coherence of earlier evidence and the distinctiveness of its contribution. Readers can use it as an entry point, but should verify its claims about prior retention evidence and situate its design alongside the earlier Louisiana adoption study.

**Strengths:**

- The review explicitly presents conflicting findings on racial diversity and high-need subject preparation, distinguishing evidence from individual programs from evidence across programs (pp. 3–4). It also acknowledges initially unfavorable effectiveness evidence from Boston rather than presenting an exclusively positive history of residencies (p. 3). These are verifiable strengths of the paper's coverage.
- The conceptual framing recognizes that residency features also occur in traditional programs and that programs adopting the label do not necessarily implement the full model (pp. 2–3). Recruitment and preparation are distinguished as potential mechanisms, and the discussion returns to the undergraduate recruitment pipeline and implementation differences when interpreting departures from previous findings (pp. 16–18). This makes the literature synthesis more informative than a simple comparison of pathway labels.
- The references combine peer-reviewed evaluations, federal multisite reports, program evaluations, and work on clinical preparation. The account also includes institutional legitimacy and isomorphism through Reagan et al. and acknowledges selection and generalizability problems in earlier comparisons (pp. 3–4). It repeatedly credits Truwit et al. (2024) for the earlier evidence on implementation and declining distinctiveness, rather than presenting those findings as newly established here.

**Weaknesses:**

- A consequential omission is Goldhaber, Xu, and Mihaly (2022), The Louisiana Believe and Prepare Educator Preparation Reform: Findings from the Pilot and Early Implementation Years. Its main report already exploits variation in implementation timing, accounts for preimplementation differences, and controls for preparation program and completion year (Box 2, pp. 5–6). It reports favorable retention associations alongside mixed instructional outcomes, including a negative ELA association that loses significance in a robustness check (pp. 7–9, Figures 1–3). This is a close predecessor to the contrast between previous research and the present within-program approach on p. 4, and supplies conflicting evidence relevant to pp. 15–18. Its absence is verifiable in the references; my judgment is that it materially weakens the novelty framing, although the present heterogeneity-robust estimator remains a meaningful distinction. [Goldhaber et al. report](https://ies.ed.gov/sites/default/files/migrated/rel/regions/southwest/pdf/REL_2023147.pdf).
- The retention synthesis gives Wan et al. (2021) more support than that source warrants. On p. 3, the article groups it under 'after 3 or more years' and says residency graduates are 'more likely to have persisted in the same district than other new teachers.' Wan et al. instead examine retention into the second year (p. 12, Figure 5), and their main text reports that differences cease to be statistically significant when comparisons are restricted by professional certification status (pp. 12–13). Thus the source supports an unadjusted descriptive advantage, with an important compositional qualification, rather than the duration and broadly favorable implication assigned to it. [Wan et al. report](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED612482.pdf).
- An and Koedel (2021) receive inconsistent descriptions concerning high-need subjects. Page 3 states that 'others reveal no differences (An & Koedel, 2021; Truwit et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2021).' Page 15 instead says that individual-program studies 'have documented higher proportions of graduates teaching in high-need subject areas than other new teachers in the same districts (An & Koedel, 2021; Papay et al., 2012).' This disagreement is directly verifiable within the article. The original Kansas City study disaggregates placements by grade and subject (pp. 12–14, Tables A1a–A1c), so readers should not repeat the later blanket characterization without specifying the comparison and subject category. [An and Koedel](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/23328584211026952).
- The review sometimes slides between district persistence and persistence in the profession: the p. 3 paragraph introduces the latter but principally summarizes the former. These outcomes have different implications for claims that Tennessee contradicts earlier retention evidence. Silva et al. (2015), for example, find a district-retention advantage but no statistically significant school-retention advantage (pp. 5–8, Figures 1–4); their design does not establish persistence anywhere in the profession. The article partially corrects this impression by discussing mobility evidence on p. 16, but its broad contrast with past retention findings still needs to be read outcome by outcome. [Silva et al. report](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/2025/01/20154015-pdf).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Read the Goldhaber, Xu, and Mihaly Louisiana report alongside this paper when assessing methodological novelty and whether adoption improves teaching or retention. Treat the Tennessee paper as an extension using a different setting, treatment definition, and estimator, rather than the first within-program adoption comparison. [Louisiana predecessor](https://ies.ed.gov/sites/default/files/migrated/rel/regions/southwest/pdf/REL_2023147.pdf).
- Use Wan et al.'s main-text certification qualification and Silva et al.'s separate school and district results when interpreting the apparent conflict with Tennessee. Keep follow-up duration, certification composition, and the geographic definition of retention explicit. [Wan et al.](https://files.eric.ed.gov/fulltext/ED612482.pdf), [Silva et al.](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/2025/01/20154015-pdf).
- For the underlying claim that residency preparation differs from traditional preparation, cite the already acknowledged Truwit, Ronfeldt, and Bardelli (2024) study. It directly documents both differences in program features and their dilution across classifications and adoption cohorts; the current paper adds outcome analyses to that implementation context. [Truwit et al.](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/pdf/10.1177/23328584241231937).
- Locate the paper principally in education policy and the economics of teacher preparation. Its institutional-isomorphism discussion offers a useful sociological connection, while qualitative accounts of professional learning, local relationships, and social justice receive less substantive treatment. The already cited Roegman et al. (2017) and Reagan et al. (2021) are appropriate companion readings for those dimensions; the administrative outcomes here should not be read as a comprehensive assessment of the educational purposes of residencies.

**Detailed Commentary:**

The rating is adequate because the paper covers major strands of the residency evidence base, acknowledges conflicting findings, and repeatedly qualifies the applicability of its results. The shortcomings are nevertheless substantive: the omitted Louisiana implementation study changes the methodological lineage, and the Wan citation and inconsistent An and Koedel descriptions reduce confidence in compressed summaries of individual studies. These findings are based on reading the entire supplied article, including its bound appendix, and targeted checks of primary sources; they do not establish that the bibliography has been exhaustively audited.

My assessment of the paper's proper contribution is narrower than a verdict on the residency model generally. The paper itself explains that its comparison concerns existing, predominantly undergraduate programs that report changing status and excludes always-residency programs from identifying the adoption effects (pp. 7–9, 17–18). Comparisons with earlier purpose-built programs therefore combine differences in research design with differences in the intervention and candidate population. That distinction is central to scholarly positioning: the findings can qualify claims about extending residency practices to existing programs without overturning earlier evidence about particular residency packages.

The interdisciplinary balance is serviceable for the stated workforce question. The paper draws on economics for identification and teacher effectiveness, on teacher-education research for clinical preparation, and on organizational sociology for diffusion. In my judgment, the thinner treatment of qualitative mechanisms limits explanation more than it undermines the existence of the quantitative contribution; a broad developmental-psychology survey would not be necessary merely to make the bibliography interdisciplinary. Online supplements and appendices not bound into the supplied article were unavailable and were not presumed to contain missing engagement. For external reports, the judgments above rely on their accessible main text and exhibits, not on unexamined separate appendices.

### Writing Review
**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The paper has a clear question, a navigable structure, and a results section that usually distinguishes suggestive findings from stronger evidence. However, conflicting subgroup counts, mislabeled figure units, an inconsistent explanation of the observation-rating scale, and several interpretations stronger than the displayed comparisons make it unsafe to rely on the abstract or discussion alone.

**Strengths:**

- The organization follows the argument effectively: model features and prior evidence precede the data and identification strategy, treatment validation precedes graduate outcomes, and the discussion separates substantive findings from interpretive limitations. Table 2 (p. 10) and Table 3 (p. 12) distinguish changes in program features from changes in graduates' outcomes; Figures 1 and 2 (pp. 11 and 13) complement these averages with event-time patterns.
- The methods explain the treatment's basis in retrospective self-identification, the distinction between transitioning and always-residency programs, and the limits of generalizing from the former to the latter (pp. 4, 7–11). The distinction is also visible in Table 1 (p. 6) and Figure A1 (p. 22), giving readers useful ways to check the prose.
- The primary-results discussion explicitly acknowledges imprecision, marginal significance, and problematic pre-trends (pp. 11–14). Its reported first-post-graduation school- and district-mobility effects of 2.6 and 1.2 percentage points agree with the displayed coefficients 0.026 and 0.012 (p. 13; Table 3, p. 12, Panel C), and its description of weak effectiveness evidence is consistent with Table 3, Panel D.
- The tables report outcome-specific sample sizes and uncertainty, while the event-study captions explain that pre-trend coefficients and treatment effects use separate regressions and reference periods (Tables 2–3, pp. 10 and 12; Figures 1–2, pp. 11 and 13). The limitations are substantive and recurring rather than relegated entirely to an endnote.

**Weaknesses:**

- Verified subgroup-count conflict: the text defines earlier adopters as 'up through 2015–2016, N = 9' and later adopters as 'in 2016–2017 or after, N = 6' (p. 14, discussion of Table A4). The table note instead states 'Earlier adopters are those (N = 6)' and 'later adopters are those (N = 9)' (Table A4, p. 21). The same paragraph on p. 14 then refers to 'the six programs adopting the model in the 2013–2014 and 2014–2015 school years.' The grouping description therefore cannot be quoted consistently from the prose and table note. This verifies a reporting conflict, not that the estimated columns themselves are reversed.
- Verified figure-unit mismatch: Figure 1's note says 'Y-axis is in percentage points' for the binary features, and Figure 2's note says 'Y-axis is measured in percentage points' for the binary outcomes (pp. 11 and 13). The plotted ticks are decimal probability changes, including '.05' and '.1', rather than percentage-point values. For example, a plotted change of .05 corresponds to five percentage points, by conversion, not .05 percentage points. Readers must rescale these axes. The small panels also use different vertical ranges, and neither caption specifies the confidence level represented by the shaded bands (Figures 1–2, pp. 11 and 13).
- Verified inconsistency in the substantive explanation of observation ratings: the methods say scores average 'across all 23 rubric items' (p. 5), whereas the discussion translates the estimated effect into 'about half a point on 1 of 15 indicators on the state rubric' (p. 15). The underlying effect is 0.032 (Table 3, p. 12, Panel D). My arithmetic check gives 0.5/15 approximately 0.033, but 0.5/23 approximately 0.022. The paper supplies no reconciliation of the different denominators, so the discussion's concrete illustration should not be repeated as an established interpretation of the measured outcome.
- Several substantive follow-ups lack a supporting exhibit in the bound paper. The special-education result is reported as '2.9 pp, 20.4% over a baseline of 14.2%, p = .019' (p. 12, prose below Table 3), but Table 3 reports only the combined high-need-endorsement outcome. Likewise, the partner-district mobility comparisons and destination-school analyses appear only in the discussion (pp. 16–17), and the covariate-adjusted checks are explicitly described as 'not reported here' (pp. 14–15). Their subgroup denominators, uncertainty, and specifications cannot be inspected as fully as the main results. This is a verification limit, not evidence that the reported findings are incorrect; unavailable online supplements cannot resolve it in this review.
- The abstract accurately identifies the Tennessee setting, predominantly undergraduate programs, reported adoption timing, and suggestive rather than definitive effectiveness and mobility findings (p. 1). However, 'we estimate the causal impacts' does not convey the pre-trend qualifications attached to the highlighted outcomes or the incompleteness of model implementation documented later (Table 2, p. 10; Table 3, p. 12; discussion, p. 14). It also omits the restriction of employment and retention measurement to Tennessee public schools. In my judgment, this compressed framing gives an abstract-only reader more confidence and a broader outcome definition than the body supports.
- The discussion sometimes converts a cautious comparison into a stronger account of how effects evolve. The methods acknowledge 'less capacity to cleanly interpret dynamic effects over time' when pooling workforce years (p. 5), but the discussion says the estimates imply that non-residency graduates 'catch up' and that residency preparation 'sets them up for an especially successful start' (p. 15). Table 3 contrasts 'First year only' with 'All available years' (p. 12); those columns do not directly display a common cohort's experience-specific convergence. Similarly, calling estimates 'lower bounds' (pp. 11 and 18) is an interpretive supposition about incomplete implementation and reporting error, not a bound demonstrated by Tables 2–3. These are judgments about the fidelity of the exposition, not claims that the proposed explanations are impossible.
- Outcome terminology occasionally exceeds the documented measurement. The operational definition is whether graduates 'failed to continue teaching in a Tennessee public school' (p. 5), but the sample description says they 'leave the profession' (p. 5), and the retention discussion speaks of persisting 'in the teaching profession' (p. 13; relevant outcome: 'Left teaching,' Table 3, p. 12). Leaving the observed state public-school workforce does not itself establish leaving teaching. Also, Table 1's row 'Ever found employment' is qualified by a note restricting workforce outcomes to 'the year immediately following graduation' (p. 6); readers need that note to avoid interpreting the row as career-long employment.
- There is an internally inconsistent attribution in the literature summary. For high-need subject areas, p. 3 says 'others reveal no differences (An & Koedel, 2021; Truwit et al., 2024; Wan et al., 2021),' whereas p. 15 says individual-program studies documented 'higher proportions of graduates teaching in high-need subject areas' and cites '(An & Koedel, 2021; Papay et al., 2012).' These passages place An and Koedel in different evidentiary categories without explanation. I have verified the conflicting descriptions within this paper, not adjudicated the cited study.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- For an efficient reading, start with the question and abstract, then read the outcome definitions and observation-window discussion on pp. 4–5, the treatment-interpretation and validation material on pp. 8–11, and Table 3 with the primary-results discussion on pp. 11–14. Read the interpretive qualifications on pp. 17–18 before using the conclusions in a policy argument.
- Use Table 3 (p. 12) as the anchor for what the main results actually establish. The p-values printed beside outcome names are pre-trend tests, as its note explains; the symbols attached to estimates concern treatment effects. Keep nonsignificant estimates distinct from demonstrated absence of an effect, and treat the proposed catch-up and lower-bound interpretations as hypotheses.
- Read Figures 1–2 (pp. 11 and 13) alongside the corresponding tables, converting binary-outcome axes from probability changes to percentage points and checking each panel's scale. Their horizontal axes represent time since program adoption, not a teacher's accumulated experience; the changing set of contributing programs is acknowledged on p. 11.
- Before quoting adoption-cohort results, compare the conflicting descriptions on p. 14 and in Table A4 (p. 21), using Figure A1 (p. 22) to inspect adoption timing. Avoid repeating either subgroup count without resolving the conflict. Likewise, quote the observation-rating coefficient from Table 3 rather than the unreconciled rubric-item illustration on p. 15.
- Do not skip the endnotes on treatment classification, retrospectively assigned partner districts, observation-rating coverage, event-study reference periods, and Title II timing (pp. 23–24). The general model background and repeated comparisons with earlier studies (pp. 2–4 and parts of pp. 15–18) can be skimmed once the question is clear; the substantive follow-ups on pp. 16–17 deserve separate, provisional treatment because their detailed exhibits are not supplied.

**Detailed Commentary:**

This assessment covers the whole supplied article, including its bound appendix, notes, and references. The key figure labels, main-results table, subgroup table, and passages underlying the numerical inconsistencies were also checked in rendered PDF pages. No external sources or other reviews were used.

The central expository strength is that readers can recover a more careful argument than the headline alone suggests. The paper distinguishes self-reported model adoption from actual feature changes and openly describes incomplete implementation, limited generalizability, and uncertainty. Its primary-results section is especially useful because it places caveats close to the affected findings. The organization therefore remains adequate despite consequential local defects.

The main navigation burden is that essential definitions are distributed across the methods, table notes, and distant endnotes, while some new substantive analyses first appear in the discussion. The exhibits are usable but not fully self-contained: Table 3 requires the methods to recover conditional populations and measurement units, and its workforce-year distinction must be read carefully. Figures 1–2 visibly display uncertainty and zero reference lines, but their caption-unit errors and unspecified shading level impede interpretation. Figure A1 offers a useful visual account of the treatment sample, yet its rows are not individually labeled, limiting how readily readers can audit the contradictory subgroup descriptions.

My rating reflects writing and presentation, not a separate judgment of methodological validity. The count reversal, axis-label mismatch, rubric-denominator discrepancy, and inconsistent citation attribution are document-verifiable reporting problems. The concerns about causal framing, career convergence, and lower bounds are interpretive judgments: the prose sometimes invites conclusions stronger than the displayed comparisons directly establish. These problems warrant careful reading and qualified quotation, while the accessible core tables and substantial caveat language keep the paper above a weak overall assessment.

### Contribution Review
**Rating:** Adequate (high confidence)

The paper adds useful evidence on what happens when existing, predominantly undergraduate teacher preparation programs in Tennessee report becoming residencies, moving beyond comparisons of graduates from different programs. Its strongest contribution is to temper expectations that such conversions reliably improve workforce diversity, employment, or retention; its positive findings on instructional effectiveness and mobility remain suggestive, and it does not identify the effects of a fully implemented residency model.

**Strengths:**

- The novel contribution is the policy-relevant comparison: changes within transitioning programs against contemporaneous changes in comparison programs, rather than simply contrasting residency graduates with other novice teachers. Linking retrospective program histories to longitudinal administrative outcomes addresses stable differences between providers that complicate the prior studies described in the paper (pp. 3–9). This is an advance in application and evidence, rather than a new statistical method.
- The paper connects residency classification to observable changes in preparation instead of treating the label as self-explanatory. Reported adoption is associated with an estimated 95.90 additional supervised clinical hours (SE 35.67; p. 10, Table 2, Panel B), alongside changes in reported program features. This makes the study informative about the incremental changes accompanying real-world adoption, even though it cannot isolate which components matter.
- The findings address consequential expectations about teacher supply and preparation. The absence of clear improvements in diversity, employment, and retention provides a useful counterweight to favorable accounts of exemplary residencies, while the separate measures of workforce exit and mobility avoid treating every school departure as a loss to the teaching workforce (p. 12, Table 3).
- The paper is unusually explicit about the population supporting its estimates: the identifying transitions come from 15 programs, while always-residency programs do not identify the adoption effects (p. 6, Table 1; p. 22, Figure A1; discussion on pp. 7–9, 18). Its discussion of undergraduate recruitment pipelines, incomplete implementation, and the spread of residency features into comparison programs helps readers interpret the restricted scope.

**Weaknesses:**

- The title's question about the model itself is only partially answered. Treatment combines partial and full self-identification and incremental changes to already evolving preparation programs; the earliest and externally recognized residencies do not supply the treatment contrast (pp. 9–11, 18, 23, note 2). The evidence therefore bears more directly on reported conversion under these conditions than on the effectiveness of the complete residency package.
- The most affirmative headline is weaker than the design's novelty might suggest. Preferred first-year effects on observation ratings and math value-added are imprecise; ELA value-added is 0.031 student-level standard deviations (SE 0.018), accompanied by a pre-trend test with p = .079 (p. 12, Table 3, Panel D). School mobility increases by 2.6 percentage points (SE 1.1 percentage points), but its pre-trend test has p = .010 (p. 12, Table 3, Panel C). These findings suggest hypotheses rather than establish dependable benefits or costs of adoption.
- Nonsignificant estimates do not establish that residencies cannot diversify or retain teachers. Limited identifying variation, imperfect adoption timing, and overlap in features across treated and comparison programs restrict what the null results can settle. The proposed interpretation as lower bounds for comprehensive implementation (pp. 11, 18) is a judgment, not an identified bound: neither stronger effects with greater implementation nor uniformly attenuating measurement error is established.
- Policy relevance exceeds the outcomes directly observed. Graduating-cohort composition does not separately identify applicant recruitment, enrollment, or completion; certification in a shortage field does not show that a shortage vacancy was filled. Employment and exits concern Tennessee public schools, and observed effectiveness concerns employed graduates with available measures (pp. 4–5). The study also provides no cost-effectiveness comparison for choosing residency expansion over other staffing policies.

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Cite this paper for evidence that reported residency conversion among existing Tennessee preparation programs did not yield clear average improvements in graduates' racial diversity, in-state public-school employment, or persistence, relative to comparison programs (p. 12, Table 3). Retain the setting and conversion qualification; do not translate these findings into proof that residencies generally have no effect.
- Cite it as a useful within-program evaluation of residency adoption and as evidence that adoption can represent modest changes in preparation features (p. 10, Table 2). Do not cite it as isolating the causal effect of yearlong placements, stipends, mentoring, or recruitment: these components are not independently identified.
- Describe the effectiveness and mobility results as suggestive and mention the imprecision and pre-trend concerns (p. 12, Table 3; p. 13, Figure 2). Smaller estimates using all available workforce years do not by themselves establish that comparison teachers catch up along a common experience trajectory, given changing follow-up and sample composition (pp. 5, 14–15).
- Open questions include whether comprehensive graduate-level or newly established residencies produce different effects, which components improve outcomes, whether partner districts gain durable staffing benefits, and whether those benefits justify program costs. The special-education and partner-district mobility analyses reported in prose (pp. 12, 16–17) are promising leads, but detailed estimates and diagnostics are not supplied in the bound exhibits. Online supplements and unbound appendices were unavailable for this review.

**Detailed Commentary:**

My assessment is that this is a valuable, bounded contribution rather than a decisive evaluation of the residency model. The document verifies a meaningful shift in research design, links reported adoption to changes in preparation, and supplies outcome estimates and robustness checks in the bound appendix. Relative to the literature as characterized on pp. 3–4, its distinctive contribution is the evaluation of conversion within existing providers. Mixed diversity findings, favorable retention claims, and some evidence of mobility already appear in that literature; those patterns are not themselves new. Applying a heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences estimator strengthens the comparison with cross-program descriptive studies, but does not remove concerns about contemporaneous changes, self-reported timing, or the adequacy of comparison trends. I have not independently established that this is the best available study across the entire literature.

For readers, the useful update is that adopting the residency label and some associated practices need not reproduce the outcomes of prominent, purpose-built residencies. That is directly relevant to leaders considering conversion, especially in undergraduate settings where the candidate pool is already largely determined. It is less informative about whether well-funded, comprehensive residencies can succeed elsewhere. The authors generally acknowledge these boundaries honestly, although the lower-bound interpretation and concluding optimism about teaching quality go beyond what is firmly established. The paper warrants an adequate contribution rating because it provides a substantive and policy-relevant advance in evidence while leaving both the comprehensive-model effect and the responsible mechanisms unresolved.

### Reproducibility Review
**Rating:** Weak (high confidence)

The paper makes its main design understandable and supplies substantial descriptive, inferential, and robustness reporting, including a bound appendix. However, the document provides no actionable route to the linked administrative and original survey data, no replication code or software environment, and incomplete instructions for constructing several central outcomes and analysis samples. These gaps prevent independent reproduction of the headline results from the reported materials, despite relatively good transparency about the statistical design.

**Strengths:**

- The data narrative identifies the Tennessee preparation-completer, personnel, and evaluation records, the original program-leader survey, and the supplementary federal Title II source. It explains the residency-classification question, the inclusion of partial residencies, exclusion of job-embedded pathways, the employment definition using personnel or evaluation records, and the conditioning of mobility on continued employment (pp. 4–5, 9–10). Treatment-history assumptions and retrospective application of partner-district identities are disclosed (p. 23, Notes 2 and 4).
- The primary specification is reasonably explicit: the displayed equation uses program and graduating-year fixed effects; untreated observations supply imputed counterfactuals; effects are aggregated for treated graduates; and inference clusters by program (pp. 7–8). The figure notes distinguish the reference observations for pre-trend coefficients and treatment effects, while Note 9 explains the equivalence the authors report between individual data and a program-by-year panel weighted by nonmissing graduate outcomes (pp. 11 and 13, Figures 1–2; p. 24, Note 9).
- The paper supplies useful reproduction targets. The descriptive sample includes 24,625 graduates across 66 programs (p. 6, Table 1), and the central school-mobility estimate is 0.026 with a standard error of 0.011 and 11,454 observations (p. 12, Table 3, Panel C, first-year column). Tables 2–3 report outcome-specific sample sizes, standard errors, and pre-trend Wald diagnostics; Tables A1–A4 report response comparisons, composition checks, alternative estimators, and adoption-cohort heterogeneity (pp. 10, 12, 19–21). These exhibits let readers inspect uncertainty and diagnostic qualifications rather than relying exclusively on the narrative.
- Important coverage limitations are disclosed, including missing evaluation observations, interrupted value-added coverage, right censoring, and uncertainty about the year represented by Title II reporting (pp. 5, 23–24, Notes 5–8 and 11–12). The main workforce analyses explicitly focus on the year immediately after graduation, and the distinction from analyses using all available workforce years is labeled in Table 3 (p. 12).

**Weaknesses:**

- There is no data-availability statement, repository, restricted-use application procedure, or documented data-use-agreement pathway in the supplied article. The acknowledgments credit TDOE and participating providers for access (p. 22), but do not explain how an independent researcher could obtain equivalent files. In particular, administrative-data access alone would not recover the original survey responses and their linkage to program identities: Figure A1 displays anonymous treatment histories without a program crosswalk (p. 22). Confidentiality can legitimately preclude public microdata; the reproducibility problem is the absence of a documented route to the necessary linked inputs.
- No analysis code, replication package, software/version information, or command options are reported. The primary model is described, but the article does not fully specify implementation choices for aggregation weights, unsupported treated observations, or finite-sample inference. The alternative estimator is identified by a methodological citation without executable settings (pp. 8, 14; p. 20, Table A3). The all-workforce-years specification also needs an explicit account of observation weighting and how graduating-year, employment-year, and experience variation enter the implementation (pp. 5, 8; p. 12, Table 3).
- A replicator would have to resolve undocumented record-construction details: the exact administrative extracts and field names, person/program linkage and duplicate-completion rules, conflicts between personnel and evaluation school identifiers, handling of multiple placements, and missing-item or multiple-score rules for evaluation measures (pp. 4–5). The paper names TVAAS and gives a technical website pointer, but does not identify the exact score fields, cross-subject/grade aggregation, or transformations used to obtain the reported value-added outcomes (p. 5; p. 13, Figure 2; p. 23, Note 6). Outcome-specific counts help identify discrepancies but do not supply a complete sample-construction audit trail.
- The adoption-subgroup documentation conflicts. The text describes 'earlier (up through 2015–2016, N = 9) and later-adopting (in 2016–2017 or after, N = 6)' programs (p. 14, discussion of Table A4). The table note instead states, 'Earlier adopters are those (N = 6) who adopted the residency model prior to the 2016–2017 school year; later adopters are those (N = 9) who adopted in 2016–2017 or after' (p. 21, Table A4). The cutoff is consistent, but the subgroup counts are reversed. This is a verifiable documentation discrepancy, not evidence establishing which grouping was actually used in estimation.
- The observation-rating description also needs reconciliation. The construction paragraph says scores average 'across all 23 rubric items for each observed lesson' (p. 5, Data), whereas the substantive interpretation refers to an increase on '1 of 15 indicators on the state rubric' (p. 15, Discussion, interpreting the observation-rating row in p. 12, Table 3). These statements may concern different rubric components, but the article supplies no crosswalk explaining their relationship; the correct item set for reproducing the outcome remains uncertain.
- Some supporting claims cannot be audited to the same standard as the main table. Covariate-adjusted robustness results are explicitly described as 'analyses not reported here' (p. 14; continued p. 15). Subject-specific endorsement findings and exploratory mobility analyses are narrated without complete corresponding coefficient, uncertainty, and sample-size tables (pp. 12, 16–17). Figures 1–2 provide graphical dynamic results but no numerical coefficient/covariance files or event-time sample counts (pp. 11, 13). The Title II timing ambiguity is acknowledged without a reproducible file-to-academic-year crosswalk (p. 24, Note 11; p. 10, Table 2).

**Guidance for Readers:**

- Before attempting replication, request an actionable TDOE access procedure, the administrative extract inventory and dictionaries, the survey instrument and deidentified response file, and a permissible program/treatment/partner-district crosswalk. Confirm that access would cover the original survey linkage as well as administrative outcomes; otherwise even the central treatment assignment cannot be independently reconstructed.
- Request data-construction and estimation scripts with software versions, and first reconcile sample counts and descriptive outcomes against Table 1 and the first-year estimates against Table 3 (pp. 6, 12). Prioritize employment-versus-evaluation linkage, missing ratings, multiple placements, observation-rating items, and value-added scaling before interpreting numerical differences as substantive failures to replicate.
- Obtain the treatment-cohort roster behind Table A4, the Title II year mapping, and exact aggregation/inference settings. Separately reproduce the all-workforce-years estimates, documenting their weighting and time indexing, before treating their comparison with first-year estimates as evidence about persistence (pp. 12, 21, Tables 3 and A4; p. 24, Note 11).
- Use the reported estimates, uncertainty, and Wald tests to assess the published main findings, but treat the covariate-adjusted, endorsement-specific, and exploratory mobility claims as only partly checkable until full results and scripts are supplied. Request numerical event-study estimates, covariance information, and contributing sample counts before relying on precise dynamic patterns (pp. 11–17, Figures 1–2 and Table 3).

**Detailed Commentary:**

This assessment is based on the complete supplied paper, including its bound appendix and endnotes; relevant equations, figures, and conflicting passages were also checked in rendered PDF pages. No external repository or access pathway was independently investigated. The absence of a sharing statement in this document does not establish that the authors possess no code or that access could never be arranged. Online supplements and appendices outside the supplied PDF were unavailable for this review, so they cannot be assumed to fill the gaps. My judgment is that the article offers adequate conceptual specification and unusually useful in-document benchmarks, but weak end-to-end reproducibility: essential treatment/linkage inputs and material construction choices remain unavailable or ambiguous even for a researcher who could obtain state records. The rating concerns verifiability as published, not whether confidential records should be publicly released, whether the estimates are necessarily wrong, or whether their causal assumptions are ultimately persuasive. The subgroup and rubric discrepancies are directly verifiable from the document; their consequences for the implemented analysis remain unknown.
